# Goals of care

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Legal medicine and professionalism > Goals of care*

[Original Article Link](/library/1E02u3)

---

## Summary

A patient's goals of care are based on their values, priorities, and preferences within a given clinical context. These goals are typically determined through <u>shared decision-making</u> and should be established and documented for any patient with an increased likelihood of <u>morbidity</u> and mortality. The care team creates a plan in collaboration with the patient by first evaluating the patient's understanding of their illness and prognosis and then discussing their values and preferences and addressing any concerns. The discussion is thoroughly documented and, if relevant, a standardized form (e.g., <u>MOLST</u>) to communicate care directives to providers and <u>health care facilities</u> is completed.




This article outlines the necessary background and steps for initiating and conducting the discussion, establishing goals of care, and appropriately documenting them. See “<u>Counseling for terminally ill patients</u>” for additional considerations.

---

## Definitions

### Goals of care [[2]](/library/WcdPYK0)




* The aim of medical care for an individual patient based on the patient's values, priorities, and preferences in a given clinical context

* Typically determined through <u>shared decision-making</u> with the patient and/or their <u>surrogate decision-maker</u>

* May also be informed by <u>advance healthcare directives</u> (see “<u>Hierarchy of medical decision-making</u>.”)

* Used to determine the overall <u>care plan</u>, including the use or avoidance of specific medical interventions





> [!TIP]
> Goals of care are dynamic and may change over time.




### <u>Medical futility</u> and potentially inappropriate treatments [[3]](/library/hqdcyI0)




This is a topic of ongoing debate and subject to varied interpretation.  [[3]](/library/hqdcyI0)




* Futile treatment: There is no universally accepted definition of <u>medical futility</u>. ;  [[4]](/library/SqdyBI0)

* This term is often used to describe interventions thought to be nonbeneficial.

* As the interpretation of benefit is subjective, its use is best limited to interventions that definitely cannot accomplish their intended physiological goal.

* In most other cases, the term “<u>potentially inappropriate treatment</u>” may be more suitable.

* Potentially inappropriate treatment

* A treatment with some chance of achieving a desired outcome for the patient, but with justifiable ethical reasons to withhold it

* Disagreements about potentially inappropriate treatments are usually value-based.

* Treatment decisions should involve <u>shared decision-making</u>, conflict resolution strategies, and expert advice (e.g., ethics consult).





### Advance care planning (<u>ACP</u>) [[5]](/library/WrdPTr0)[[6]](/library/drdoTr0)




* The act of clarifying and documenting desired future goals of care, usually through a legal process.

* Typically, the aim is to communicate the patient's wishes to treating teams and loved ones in case they lose <u>decision-making capacity</u>.

* Although <u>ACP</u> is sometimes used interchangeably with <u>goals of care discussions</u> because the processes overlap, there are some differences.

* <u>ACP</u> is more commonly codified in legal documents that clinicians cannot draft (e.g., <u>advance directives</u>, <u>medical power of attorney</u>).

* Although clinicians are usually consulted and often initiate <u>ACP</u> discussions, patients can document their <u>ACP</u> alone or via a legal representative (e.g., a notary) without clinician involvement.

---

## Limitation of life-sustaining treatment

### Definitions




* Life-sustaining treatment (LST): interventions aimed at prolonging life

* Limitation of LST: the avoidance or discontinuation of an LST when it is no longer thought to help achieve the goals of care [[7]](/library/ZmdZVq0)[[8]](/library/VcdGYK0)

* Withdrawing LST: discontinuing an LST (e.g., extubating a mechanically-ventilated patient, discontinuing artificial feeding for a patient in a <u>persistent vegetative state</u>)

* Withholding LST: avoiding intensifying a current treatment or initiating a new treatment (see “Orders for limiting LST” for examples).

* May be requested at any time by a patient or their <u>surrogate decision-maker</u>

* May be initiated by the medical team if an LST is considered a <u>potentially inappropriate treatment</u>

* Comfort-focused care: <u>end-of-life care</u> aimed at prioritizing symptomatic relief and patient comfort over curative or life-sustaining therapies [[9]](/library/sodtWI0) 

* Often limits, but does not preclude the use of invasive or life-sustaining treatment

* See also “<u>Comfort measures only</u>” and “<u>Palliative care</u>.”





> [!TIP]
> With fully <u>informed consent</u>, a patient or their <u>surrogate decision-maker</u> can refuse treatment at any time, even if this results in the patient's <u>death</u>. [[7]](/library/ZmdZVq0)[[8]](/library/VcdGYK0)




### Orders for limiting LST




Orders for limiting LST are generally determined through <u>shared decision-making</u> with the patient and/or <u>surrogate decision-maker</u>.




* No escalation of treatment (<u>NEOT</u>): an order to continue ongoing treatment but avoid new or intensified treatment  [[10]](/library/7TW4Hk0)

* Code status: orders designating which resuscitation efforts should be made in the event of cardiac and/or <u>respiratory arrest</u> [[11]](/library/MbXM89)[[12]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[13]](/library/1cd2YK0)

* <u>Full code</u>: Make all efforts to resuscitate.

* Do not intubate (<u>DNI</u>): Withhold <u>endotracheal intubation</u>.

* Do not resuscitate (<u>DNR</u>): Withhold <u>CPR</u> or <u>advanced cardiac life support</u> in the case of <u>cardiac arrest</u>.

* <u>DNR</u> and <u>DNI</u> (DNR/DNI): Withhold both <u>CPR</u> and <u>endotracheal intubation</u>.

* Comfort measures only: commonly used as an order set or a level of care designation [[9]](/library/sodtWI0)[[14]](/library/sKdt3I0)[[15]](/library/GKdB3I0)

* Typically meant to allow for a natural dying process while ensuring maximum comfort [[16]](/library/tKdXRI0)

* Should not be used as a standalone order, as it is poorly defined and interpretation varies [[9]](/library/sodtWI0)

* Instead, include orders for specific comfort-promoting measures and indicate interventions to avoid.

* See also “<u>Comfort-focused care</u>” and “<u>Management of imminently dying patients</u>.”

* Do not hospitalize. [[17]](/library/LKdwSI0)[[18]](/library/LidwHp0)

* For patients in long-term care facilities or at home

* Aims to reduce risk of <u>iatrogenic harm</u> and improve comfort near the end of life

* Perioperative <u>advance directives</u> [[19]](/library/0nde7q0)

* Procedure-specific directives specify which procedures (e.g., <u>intubation</u>, <u>chest compressions</u>, <u>defibrillation</u>) are to be allowed or avoided perioperatively.

* Goal-directed directives specify the patient's perioperative goals of care and allow appropriate resuscitation procedures to be determined by the physician.

* Typically used in patients with a <u>DNR</u> and/or <u>DNI order</u> who require <u>general anesthesia</u> for a surgical procedure

* Apply only for a defined perioperative period, after which the original <u>code status</u> order goes back into effect





### Ethical and medicolegal issues [[20]](/library/lrdvhr0)




* Decisions to withhold or <u>withdraw LST</u> are challenging and can pose ethical dilemmas, especially when <u>goals of care discussions</u> or advanced care planning have not yet occurred.

* Laws governing <u>withdrawal of LST</u> vary by region and clinical circumstances, e.g., <u>brain death</u> or <u>persistent vegetative state</u>.

* Disagreements can arise due to:

* Medical advances that affect survival and recovery

* Challenges with accurate prognostication

* Varied interpretations of <u>medical futility</u> and <u>potentially inappropriate treatment</u>

* Differences in cultural and religious beliefs

* Consult a medical ethicist early if there is uncertainty or potential for disagreement.

* Whenever possible, discuss and document in advance the circumstances in which a patient or <u>surrogate decision-maker</u> wishes to <u>withdraw LST</u>.

* See also “<u>Ethical issues concerning brain death</u>.”

## Indications

* <u>Goals of care discussions</u> may occur at any time.

* The following situations should prompt a more urgent discussion: [[12]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[21]](/library/ecdxYK0)[[22]](/library/andQ7q0)

* High likelihood of <u>death</u> within a year (e.g., <u>advanced cancer</u> or late-stage chronic disease)

* Older patients who are seen in the emergency department and/or admitted to the hospital for serious illness

* Anticipated need for critical care

* Acute clinical deterioration

* Conditions requiring investigations and/or treatments that are high risk, painful, invasive, and/or have a low likelihood of success





> [!TIP]
> Goals of care should ideally be addressed as part of advanced care planning during health and/or early in the disease course, and repeatedly reevaluated as the clinical situation changes.




> [!TIP]
> <u>Code status</u> should be confirmed with the patient, their <u>advance directives</u>, and/or their <u>surrogate decision-maker</u> at each hospital admission. [[12]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

## Technique/steps

### Using communication strategies




Examples of communication strategies that can be used to guide the conversation include:




* <u>Ask-tell-ask</u>

* <u>SPIKES protocol</u>

* REMAP framework [[23]](/library/1nd2Hq0)

* Reframe: Clarify the medical situation.

* Expect emotion: Anticipate and validate the patient's emotional response.

* Map out goals: Ask <u>open-ended questions</u> about what matters most to the patient.

* Align with goals: Explicitly reflect your understanding of the patient’s values and goals.

* Propose a plan: Create a <u>care plan</u> that aligns with these goals.

* Also see “<u>Breaking bad news</u>” and “<u>Management of challenges in goals of care discussions</u>.”





> [!TIP]
> Employ understandable language tailored to the cultural background, education level, and emotional state of the patient and their loved ones. [[24]](/library/1rd2Tr0)




### Establishing a common understanding [[12]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[21]](/library/ecdxYK0)[[22]](/library/andQ7q0)




* Verify preferred roles in decision-making.

* Review prior discussions of medical conditions and health care preferences.

* Assess understanding of current illness and prognosis and willingness to receive more information.

* Explain current treatment measures and prognosis.

* Ask about expectations, worries, fears, and hopes.





### Establishing values and goals [[12]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[21]](/library/ecdxYK0)[[22]](/library/andQ7q0)




* Explore the patient's values, priorities (e.g., acceptable health states), goals, and preferences.

* Review treatment and intervention options.

* Make recommendations based on the patient's expressed preferences and goals.

* Address <u>code status</u> when appropriate.

* Summarize and confirm understanding and agreement with the treatment plan.





> [!TIP]
> Avoid rushing patients to make concrete decisions if they are not ready. Allow time to process and cope with difficult circumstances and bad news. [[24]](/library/1rd2Tr0)




### Supporting decisions to <u>limit life-sustaining treatment</u> [[12]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[21]](/library/ecdxYK0)[[22]](/library/andQ7q0)




* Involve <u>palliative care</u> services if necessary.

* Consider referral for <u>hospice care</u> in patients with limited <u>life expectancy</u> and with limitation of LST orders.

* Provide additional information and assistance as appropriate (e.g., referral for <u>chaplain</u> services, <u>psychosocial counseling</u>).

* See also “<u>Counseling for terminally ill patients</u>” and “<u>Spiritual care and counseling</u>.”
